title: MPs clash over Sunday sitting as marathon study of Carney's major projects bill continues
summary: With the knock of a gavel and an F-bomb, a House of Commons committee briefly went off the rails as MPs argued about overtime sittings on the Carney government's latest major projects legislation.

image.caption: James Maloney, the chair of the special bill C-39 committee, makes his way to a caucus meeting on Parliament Hill, in Ottawa, on Wednesday, Dec. 3, 2025. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: With the knock of a gavel and an F-bomb, a House of Commons committee briefly went off the rails as MPs argued about overtime sittings on the Carney government's latest major projects legislation.
"This is f--king stupid, come on," committee chair James Maloney said on Thursday afternoon.
Conservatives accused Maloney of blindsiding them by forcing study of Bill C-39 until midnight through the weekend including Sunday, which is the Sabbath for Christians.
It's rare for the House of Commons or a parliamentary committee to meet on the weekend.
'This is f--king stupid,' says Liberal MP as committee gets heated
"We just received notices of meeting for Saturday and Sunday," said Conservative MP Phil Lawrence.
"I have multiple constituency events. I also attend church … so if you want to violate my religious principles you go ahead and do that."
His colleague, Conservative Dan Albas, said some members have religious obligations and maybe even confession, in what appeared to be veiled criticism of Liberal members.

items: Canadawide Bill C-39 protests hit Thunder Bay

blocks.text: Maloney responded by saying that the sitting schedule for the committee was well known and not a surprise.
"I too go to church," Maloney said. He added that he takes "great offence" to any assertion that he was springing the weekend meetings on members.
After suspending for a couple of minutes, the committee continued its work.
Liberals keep 'nearly royal powers': Bloc MP
This was one of several tense moments over the past few days.

Opposition MPs attempted earlier Thursday to restrain the extraordinary and permanent powers the Carney government wants to give itself to override federal laws to advance mines, pipelines and other major projects.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is seen at the APEC summit in China on Thursday. Back in Ottawa, his government's new major projects bill is being studied by a special committee. (Ng Han Guan/Pool/The Associated Press)

Liberals hold the majority of votes on the special committee studying the Building Canada Strong Act. They overruled attempts by other MPs to protect the sunset clause in the Carney government's previous major projects legislation.
Bill C-39 removes the 2030 expiration date for cabinet's broad powers to override regulations and laws that are part of Bill C-5, which passed last year.
MPs have sat until midnight for the last three days, going through the bill line by line.
The Conservatives, Bloc Québécois, NDP and Greens all attempted to protect the sunset clause.
"Conservatives do believe in limited government," said Albas. "We don't believe the executive [cabinet] should have unbridled power without any parliamentary scrutiny."
He said the removal of the sunset clause is "a big mistake" and "to the detriment of our Parliament."
Liberal MP speaks out over party's major project fast-tracking legislation C-39
Environmentalists fear Ottawa could exempt major projects from laws such as the Species At Risk Act, which protects animals and other wildlife from going extinct.
Similarly, MPs have raised concerns that Canada's national parks could become casualties of the government's need for speed if cabinet decides to exempt projects from the Canada National Parks Act.

items: Carney government tweaks controversial bill to fast-track pipelines and mines

blocks.text: Bloc MP Jean-Denis Garon accused Prime Minister Mark Carney of attempting to give himself "undemocratic" and "nearly royal powers."

Two projects are in line to benefit from the measure: the Pacific Link pipeline, which would carry Alberta bitumen to the West Coast, and the proposed port facility where that pipeline would likely terminate: Robert Banks Terminal Two.

The Carney government's Major Projects Office is tasked with helping both projects along. Answering questions from MPs, Sarah Jackson, one of the directors for the office, said Bill C-39 gives certainty to projects that are not time limited.
It also "enables the project to proceed to that next step where investors may have been unable to do so otherwise," Jackson told the committee.
Regions of national interest
The Carney government is also seeking powers to advance major projects over large geographical regions.
On Wednesday night, opposition parties narrowed in on that part of the bill, which grants cabinet a new tool to create regions of national interest.
That measure would allow Ottawa to preapprove mines, pipelines, power lines and other activities over a large area.

items: Water, toxic waste and opportunity: Indigenous leaders react to Carney's pipeline plan

blocks.text: Liberals underline, however, that designation would only follow broad study of an area through a regional assessment.

Such a study is essentially an environmental assessment of the region under consideration. One is currently underway in the Ring of Fire, a mineral-rich and ecologically sensitive area of northern Ontario.
Bill C-39 represents 'mass dilution' of First Nations rights, nature protections: AFN national chief

Liberal MP Danielle Martin said this study would help communities better understand the impacts of resource development on wildlife, lands and waters — essentially "what the potential for projects might be in a region and what parts not to touch."
Similarly to maintaining the sunset clause, Liberals declined to implement calls for more guardrails and transparency around regions of national interest.
As it stands there are no limits to the amount of land or water that could fall under these new powers.

items: Liberal MP calls for more safeguards in Bill C-39
Critics accuse Carney government of proposing 'sacrifice zones'

blocks.text: Conservatives said at committee they are broadly supportive of the regional designations but attempted to introduce limits on the power of ministers.
Amendments introduced by Conservative MP Branden Leslie required that cabinet can only choose areas that contribute to international trade, energy security, critical minerals and national defence.
Leslie also attempted to get a measure that requires the government to release a map of the area under consideration before cabinet makes a decision.

"Show us the map. Tell us what projects would qualify. Explain the expected benefits for Canada," said Leslie. "Why a whole region is needed and why those boundaries make sense. Not crazy information for the government to provide."

A joint statement on Thursday from the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs and environmental groups note that few opposition amendments have been accepted, and most pertaining to Indigenous rights and free prior and informed consent have also been rejected.

"Bill C-39 and Canada's irresponsible, rushed legislative process represent an unacceptable erosion of accountability and a direct threat to reconciliation" said the president of the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs, Grand Chief Stewart Phillip.
